prize_parts.citation: for a body of work that renews poetry, the essay and the book itself, joining exacting classical learning to grief and desire in original verse narrative, elegy and essay

statement.case_for: My laureate does not change after the exchange, but I have sharpened the credit. The strongest case for Carson rests on a small set of original works that are widely discussed and that I know from public information, not fresh reading: Eros the Bittersweet, Short Talks, Autobiography of Red, The Beauty of the Husband, Nox, Decreation and the sequel Red Doc>. I would name these as the credited core, with the classical versions as context and not as the credited achievement. Across them the voice stays recognisable and the form changes: essay on desire, short prose-poem, verse novel, marriage-and-betrayal sequence, elegy as object. The recurring practice is to take an inherited form or fragment and reshape it until the form itself carries grief or desire. That gives distinctiveness of voice, formal achievement, and imaginative and intellectual depth, and the span of decades supports sustained quality. Her English removes one translation uncertainty. That reduces what I cannot judge but does not add merit, and I do not count it as merit. I also take the chair's point that my opening rank is not evidence. My view rests on the arguments about the work, not on how many members ranked her first. The citation I now propose names the emotional pull and the original genres, so that it credits what the books do and not their apparatus.
statement.case_against: The reservations I take most seriously are three. First, there is no single title that the whole committee would accept as the unquestioned centre, and a citation for the whole oeuvre should not imply more consensus about canonical weight than exists. Second, the delimitation problem is real. Even with the credit narrowed to original work, parts of the corpus depend on translation, adaptation, performance or physical design, and a text-only reading may misjudge them. Third, Cărtărescu's project is easier to state in one sentence, and Mattson and Olsson are right that this counts for the clarity of the whole-oeuvre claim. If a close reading of the later books showed that they repeat the early devices and do not extend them, my case would weaken materially, and I would regard Cărtărescu as the stronger candidate on sustained quality. I have not seen any expert reports or fresh readings in this exchange, so I cannot say how that test would come out.

responses.point: The chair holds Cărtărescu first and Carson second because his project has a more stable centre, and because Carson's genre-crossing practice and the translation and scholarship component make a whole-oeuvre citation harder to draw cleanly. He also asks for a common reading of the will's 'idealistic direction'.
responses.response: I accept that the delimitation problem is a real cost and not just a drafting issue, and I have changed my citation in response: it now names original verse narrative, elegy and essay as the credited achievement. On the will, I propose the reading several of us already use, seriousness of purpose and ethical and emotional depth, and I would apply it to both leading candidates. On that reading I cannot say Cărtărescu's metaphysical cosmology fits better than Carson's treatment of loss and the claims of the past. If the committee instead reads the wording as favouring epic or visionary ambition, that would favour him, and I would say so openly. I do not think the wording settles the choice. Your distinction that his open questions concern reading quality while hers concern corpus boundaries is fair. I think a narrower citation resolves hers more fully than anything can resolve translation dependence in his.

responses.point: Mattson argues that Cărtărescu's project can be stated in one sentence and sustained across decades, while Carson's range across modes leaves no single defining achievement. She also says a case for him needs evidence that his late work extends the earlier vocabulary, which neither she nor Olsson can confirm in Romanian.
responses.response: I cannot make the one-sentence claim for Carson as cleanly, and I will not pretend I can. The nearest statement I can defend is a practice and not a project: an inherited form made to carry present grief and desire by reshaping the form. I think that is a real unity, but a less compact one than a single metaphysical architecture, and I accept that this is a difference in how legible the oeuvre is. Your request for evidence about Cărtărescu's late novels is the right test, and it applies in parallel to me. I would not support Carson on the claim that her later books extend the early ones unless someone with closer knowledge tests Red Doc> and the later collections against Autobiography of Red. Both cases currently depend on an unverified claim about late work, and the committee should say so.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg prefers Carson but says he would not object if the committee moved to Cărtărescu on epic scale. He also says agreement among Carson's supporters is not evidence of merit, and that the readership objection must be answered on literary grounds.
responses.response: I agree on the first point, and I take your concession seriously, because it shows the question is whether scale should outweigh formal range. I do not think it should decide the matter alone, but I cannot show that it should not. On readership I will answer on literary grounds, as you ask. The relevant question is whether the allusive apparatus is a gate or a source of the emotional force, and in Nox the elegy seems to me available without classical training, but that is a judgment from public knowledge and I flag it as such. I would not use agreement among the four of us as an argument, and I am treating the vote tally the same way.

responses.point: Palm asks whether Carson's breadth is range or diffusion, and says the hybrid book-objects may be influential mainly among peers. She also puts the weight on formal economy and compressed lyric invention, against Olsson's weight on large-scale cosmology.
responses.response: Your own raising of the diffusion risk is useful, because it gives the committee a concrete test: do the later books deepen the same concern, or repeat the early devices? I would run that test before any vote. I share your weighting toward compression and formal economy, but I would not state it as a general criterion that disadvantages scale as such, since Cărtărescu's scale is a legitimate mode of achievement. On peer influence versus canon, I still cannot settle durability, and I think no member can. I am therefore relying on the quality of the present achievement, as in round 1.

responses.point: Sward would anchor a Carson citation in the written text and treat Nox's physical form as an extension and not a substitute, and says her preference over Cărtărescu is a difference of weighting she cannot fully resolve.
responses.response: I accept the scope you propose, and my revised citation is compatible with it: 'the book itself' appears there as renewal of the form through original genres, not as a claim about design or performance. I agree that text-only assessment leaves part of Nox outside what the committee can judge, and that gap should be stated openly in the discussion. I am in the same position on weighting: after this exchange I do not think the difference between unity of project and breadth of reinvention can be resolved by further argument, only by closer reading of the later work on both sides.

uncertainties: Whether Carson's later and more performance-oriented work, including Red Doc> and later collections, sustains the level of Autobiography of Red and Nox. I cannot independently verify this and I have not seen any expert report.

How to word a Carson citation so that it credits original poetry, verse narrative and essays and not the translations and versions of ancient texts. I propose a narrower credit but do not consider the boundary fully settled.
Whether the object-based and performance-linked works can be judged fairly from text and description alone.

Whether the committee will read the will's 'idealistic direction' as seriousness of purpose, as I do, or as favouring epic or visionary ambition. The two readings could change the comparison with Cărtărescu.

For Cărtărescu, translation fidelity of dense Romanian prose, uneven coverage of his early poetry and shorter fiction, and whether the late novels extend or repeat the earlier project. For Wright, whether a small number of major novels can establish sustained quality.
My knowledge rests on general public information, not fresh reading, and I do not claim to have verified any source.
Whether the co-opted member votes in committee is undocumented, and my simulated vote is a modeling assumption.
statement.conflict_note: No tie to any shortlisted writer is recorded in the supplied profile, and none is apparent. Her own work is biography and non-fiction, and that is context only, not evidence of a preference. The profile records that she became Permanent Secretary on 1 June 2026 and is expected to announce the laureate. That is an institutional role and not a tie to a candidate. As the chair's summary notes, she is one of the four explicit B002 preferences while her committee voting status is undocumented, so any weight placed on her vote is a modeling assumption.
